Balance of Plant

Role and Scope

The balance of plant (BOP) includes the non-electrical auxiliary equipment required to operate the PEM electrolyser stack safely and continuously. In this model, the BOP manages feedwater supply, heat removal, gas-liquid separation, hydrogen drying, hydrogen-side piping, instrumentation and housing.

Because the system is offshore, the feedwater system must also include seawater intake, desalination and final purification to electrolyser-grade water.

Power electronics are excluded completely because the required components depend on the electrical architecture. Transformers, rectifiers and other electrical conversion equipment are discussed on Electrolyser Power Electronics.

The stack, compressors, hydrogen export system, offshore installation, offshore structures and indirect project costs are also represented elsewhere in the model.

The scope used in this page is therefore:

Scope boundary for the balance-of-plant model.
Included in this BOP model Excluded from this BOP model
Thermal management PEM electrolyser stack
Feedwater handling Power electronics
Seawater intake Transformers and rectifiers
Desalination and final purification Hydrogen compression
Gas-liquid separation Hydrogen export system
Hydrogen drying Offshore foundations and structures
Hydrogen-side BOP piping Offshore installation
Instrumentation and housing Site preparation and indirect costs

Key Assumptions

The main assumptions used in the base-case BOP model are:

Main base-case assumptions for the BOP model.
Parameter Base value Comment
Non-water non-electrical BOP reference cost 333 2020 USD/kW NREL 1,000 MW/year case plus 50% manufacturer markup
Offshore water treatment placeholder 63 2020 USD/kW NREL water supply value plus 50% manufacturer markup
Reference capacity 1 MW NREL reference system
Scaling exponent 0.6 Six-tenths rule
BOP electricity consumption 1.0 kWh/kg H₂ Excludes compression and power electronics

These assumptions should be interpreted as early-stage modelling values. The NREL reference system is a land-based 1 MW manufactured-cost estimate. Applying it to offshore multi-MW or GW-scale systems introduces uncertainty because offshore systems require different packaging, redundancy, corrosion protection, maintainability, water intake, cooling strategy and safety zoning. The scaling exponent captures generic economies of scale, but it does not represent a detailed offshore process design.

Cost Basis

Scope of Cost Estimate

The non-electrical BOP cost is based on the NREL PEM electrolyser manufactured cost analysis. NREL reports subsystem costs for a 1 MW PEM electrolyser system in 2020 USD per kW of electrolyser capacity.1

The base case uses the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case because the offshore hydrogen system considered here represents industrial-scale deployment rather than early low-volume manufacturing.

Electrical BOP is excluded from the NREL cost breakdown. The NREL water supply category is also separated from the generic BOP cost because offshore seawater treatment requires an explicit desalination and purification model.

This page distinguishes between three cost levels:

Cost levels used to interpret the BOP estimate.
Cost level Meaning Treatment in this model
Manufactured cost Factory production cost reported by NREL Used as the starting point
Equipment purchase cost Manufactured cost plus manufacturer markup Used for the BOP reference cost
Installed offshore cost Equipment cost plus installation, structures, offshore logistics, contingency and indirect costs Excluded here and represented elsewhere

NREL Reference Cost

The remaining non-water, non-electrical BOP manufactured costs used in the base case are:

Non-water non-electrical BOP manufactured costs from the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case.
Subsystem Manufactured cost [2020 USD/kW]
Thermal management 61
Hydrogen processing 88
Hydrogen-side BOP 4
Piping, instrumentation and housing 69
Total non-water non-electrical BOP 222

A manufacturer markup of 50% is applied to convert manufactured cost into an approximate equipment purchase cost. The resulting marked-up non-water BOP reference cost is:

[ c_ = 1.5 = 333  ]

For the 1 MW NREL reference system, this corresponds to:

[ C_ = 333{,}000  ]

This value excludes power electronics, stack costs, offshore water treatment, installation, offshore structures, site preparation, indirect costs, inflation and offshore-specific cost adders.

Offshore Water Treatment

The offshore water treatment system converts seawater into the high-purity water required by the PEM electrolyser. This system includes seawater intake, coarse filtration, desalination, polishing and deionisation.

The cost is represented separately because the NREL water supply category is not assumed to fully capture offshore seawater desalination and purification.

The offshore water treatment reference cost is defined as:

[ C_]

where (C_) is the marked-up cost of the water treatment system for a 1 MW electrolyser reference unit.

If no dedicated offshore desalination cost estimate is available, the NREL water supply value may be used only as a placeholder and should be clearly labelled as incomplete. In the NREL 1,000 MW/year case, the water supply manufactured cost is 42 2020 USD/kW. Applying the same 50% manufacturer markup gives a placeholder value of:

[ c_ = 1.5 = 63  ]

For the 1 MW reference system, this corresponds to:

[ C_ = 63{,}000  ]

when the placeholder value is used.

This placeholder should be replaced by a desalination and ultrapure-water treatment cost estimate when available. The water treatment cost is kept separate so that offshore-specific assumptions can be tested independently from the rest of the BOP.

Scaling Method

The BOP is not assumed to scale linearly with installed capacity. Water treatment, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, piping and instrumentation can be shared across multiple stacks. A centralised or semi-centralised BOP system is therefore expected to be cheaper than many small independent BOP systems with the same total capacity.

Because the exact scaling exponent is not known, the model uses the six-tenths rule as a first-order process-equipment scaling approximation.2

For a BOP unit with capacity (P_i), the non-water BOP cost is calculated as:

[ C_{,i} = C_ ( )^{0.6}]

where (P_=1  ) is the NREL reference capacity.

The offshore water treatment cost is scaled separately:

[ C_{,i} = C_ ( )^{0.6}]

The total BOP cost is calculated by summing the non-water BOP and offshore water treatment costs over all independent BOP units:

[ C_ = _i ]

This formulation allows the model to distinguish between decentralised and centralised electrolyser architectures.

Under this scaling assumption, a more centralised BOP architecture is cheaper than a highly decentralised architecture with the same total electrolyser capacity. In practice, the optimum is likely to involve several shared BOP trains rather than one fully centralised unit, because redundancy, maintainability and safety constraints limit the practical size of individual BOP systems.

The scaling rule should therefore be interpreted as an early-stage approximation rather than a detailed equipment design. Future work may replace this rule with a process-level BOP model for seawater intake, desalination, deionisation, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying and hydrogen-side piping.

Manufacturing Volume Sensitivity

The base case uses the 1,000 MW/year NREL manufacturing-volume case. The 10 MW/year and 100 MW/year NREL cases may be used in sensitivity analysis to represent less mature supply chains or slower industrial scale-up.

After excluding electrical BOP and separating water supply, the non-water BOP sensitivity values are:

Manufacturing-volume sensitivity for the non-water non-electrical BOP cost.
Manufacturing volume Non-water non-electrical BOP manufactured cost [2020 USD/kW] With 50% markup [2020 USD/kW]
10 MW/year 296 444
100 MW/year 265 398
1,000 MW/year 222 333

The selected manufacturing-volume case changes (C_), while the six-tenths rule determines how this reference cost scales with the size of each shared BOP unit.

The offshore water treatment cost is controlled separately through (C_), because desalination and ultrapure-water polishing depend on offshore water quality, redundancy requirements and the selected treatment process.

BOP Power Consumption

The BOP also consumes electricity during electrolyser operation. This consumption is treated separately from stack electricity consumption.

The BOP power consumption represents parasitic loads from auxiliary systems such as pumps, fans, chillers, recirculation blowers, thermal management and hydrogen drying.

Compression is excluded from this value because compression is represented elsewhere in the model. Electrical conversion losses are also explicitly excluded because power electronics are represented separately.

The NREL report cites a generic BOP electricity consumption of 4.2 kWh/kg H₂, but this value includes electrical losses and is therefore not directly applicable to the non-electrical BOP scope used here.3

The underlying Ruth and Ahluwalia source separates BOP losses into electrical, mechanical and hydrogen-related losses. After excluding electrical losses, the remaining BOP consumption is:

Non-electrical BOP electricity consumption after excluding electrical losses.
Operating point Mechanical [kWh/kg H₂] Hydrogen [kWh/kg H₂] Total [kWh/kg H₂]
Rated power, BOL 1.3 0.2 1.5
Rated power, EOL 2.3 0.2 2.5
Minimum-loss point, BOL 0.4 0.1 0.5
Minimum-loss point, EOL 0.6 0.1 0.7

A simple lifetime average gives approximately 2.0 kWh/kg H₂ at rated power and 0.6 kWh/kg H₂ at the minimum-loss operating point. The difference is mainly caused by thermal management. At the minimum-loss operating point, the stack operates more efficiently and therefore produces less waste heat. Lower waste heat reduces the cooling duty and associated mechanical power consumption.

In this study, the stack is deliberately oversized so that the electrolyser usually operates closer to the minimum-loss point than to rated stack operation. The model therefore assumes an average non-electrical BOP power consumption of:

[ e_ = 1.0  ]

This value includes mechanical BOP loads and hydrogen drying losses. It is selected as a conservative average. It is higher than the minimum-loss values reported by Ruth and Ahluwalia to allow for offshore cooling, water handling, drying, control systems, part-load operation and uncertainty in auxiliary loads.

Desalination

Offshore desalination and water polishing are small compared with the main BOP parasitic loads. A worst-case reverse-osmosis electricity use of 5.0 kWh/m³ corresponds to approximately 0.05 kWh/kg H₂ when 10 L of water is required per kg H₂. This is small relative to the assumed 1.0 kWh/kg H₂ BOP consumption.

Desalination power is therefore included within the BOP power allowance unless a separate water-treatment model is used.

The total BOP electricity consumption is calculated as:

[ E_ = e_ m_]

where (E_) is the BOP electricity consumption and (m_) is the hydrogen production.

The assumed value of (e_) should be interpreted as an average value for an oversized offshore PEM electrolyser operating predominantly away from rated stack power.

Model Limitations

This BOP model is intended for early-stage techno-economic assessment. It should not be interpreted as a detailed offshore BOP design.

The main limitations are:

Main limitations of the current BOP model.
Limitation Implication
Land-based NREL cost data are used as the cost basis Offshore packaging, redundancy, corrosion protection and maintainability are not explicitly costed
A generic 0.6 scaling exponent is used The model captures broad economies of scale but not detailed equipment train sizing
Offshore water treatment uses a placeholder value when no dedicated estimate is available Desalination and ultrapure-water costs should be updated when project-specific data are available
BOP electricity consumption is represented by a single average value Dynamic behaviour, thermal transients and detailed part-load operation are not modelled
Compression is excluded Any compression energy and cost must be added elsewhere in the model

Future work should replace the generic scaling approach with a process-level BOP model that separately estimates seawater intake, desalination, deionisation, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, hydrogen-side piping, redundancy and offshore packaging.

  3. NREL, Updated Manufactured Cost Analysis for Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolyzers, NREL/TP-6A20-87625, Table 1.↩︎
